name: Accounting for Decentralised Treasuries
title: Accounting for Decentralised Treasuries
answer: Accounting for decentralised treasuries covers the recording, valuation, and reporting of assets held by DAOs, protocol treasuries, and other on-chain entities that manage funds through smart contracts and multisig wallets. It includes native tokens, stablecoins, wrapped assets, liquidity positions, loans, and governance tokens held across multiple chains. The work sits within digital asset accounting because these treasuries do not have conventional bank statements or a single administrator, so the accountant must reconstruct economic activity from blockchain data.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Accounting for decentralised treasuries covers the recording, valuation, and reporting of assets held by DAOs, protocol treasuries, and other on-chain entities that manage funds through smart contracts and multisig wallets. It includes native tokens, stablecoins, wrapped assets, liquidity positions, loans, and governance tokens held across multiple chains. The work sits within digital asset accounting because these treasuries do not have conventional bank statements or a single administrator, so the accountant must reconstruct economic activity from blockchain data.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The underlying infrastructure is the set of blockchains, wallet addresses, smart contracts, and multisig arrangements that hold and move treasury assets. Accountants typically pull data from block explorers, indexers, and subgraphs, then feed it into accounting software or spreadsheets that can handle token transfers, swaps, and yield events. Because a treasury may operate on Ethereum, Solana, or layer-two networks, the infrastructure must reconcile the same economic entity across many addresses and chains.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by first defining the treasury's scope, such as which wallets and contracts belong to the reporting entity, then mapping every transaction to an accounting event. Transfers between the treasury's own wallets are reclassified as internal movements, while inflows from protocol fees, grants, or token sales are recognised as revenue or capital depending on their nature. Outflows for grants, payroll, or buybacks are matched to expense or treasury management categories, and positions in liquidity pools or lending markets are marked to market or valued using observable on-chain prices at period end.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance centre on who controls the treasury and how decisions are authorised, because many decentralised treasuries are governed by token holder votes or multisig signers rather than a board. Accountants must preserve evidence of governance proposals, multisig approvals, and transaction hashes to support the ownership and authorisation of each movement. Key risks include key compromise, smart contract failure, bridge exploits, and unclear legal ownership, all of which can change whether an asset should be recognised on the balance sheet or disclosed as a contingent item.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Where it is going is toward more automated reconciliation and real-time reporting as treasury management tools and accounting software converge. Standard setters and auditors are gradually developing guidance for on-chain assets, which will push treasuries to adopt consistent valuation and disclosure practices. Over time, expect more treasuries to publish machine-readable financial statements directly from their wallets, with accounting systems able to verify balances and flows against the chain rather than relying on manual exports.
